clock_text: Thursday, May 7, 2026, 2:00 PM, US Eastern time
text:
The sash's ragged thread still knots at my palm; two days' stitchmarks map the skin.

The flick is small. A bright edge of brass, turned once under the chandler's overhang, then gone. I count from it. One. Two. Three. The gap closes on the next pile's creak, and the coin's nick, pressed against my thumb, warms as if held. Vesh has marked the datum. The folio has been read.

I keep to the eaves and count the lane by stone. Eleven paces to the bollard. Six along the wall. At the hook above the water stair, where a rope is belayed to an iron ring, I stop and lay two fingers on its lay.

Renn's tracer sits there, a loop of waxed cord drawn round the hook and cinched flat. The knot is a single turn and a tuck, pulled so tight that the tar has softened under it and hardened again. The loose end runs toward the bridge, no thicker than a hair, along the mortar where a hand would not catch it. I follow it with my nail. The cord is taut, and its chill climbs into the first joint of my finger and stays there.

I run the rule along the course until its bone edge touches the seam. It leads north and west, past the drain grate, along the lower wall to the bridge's foot. I walk it the way I would walk a chain, one stone, one breath.

The lamp at the bridge hisses through its crack. Under the planks the piles groan, and the span gives back a finger's width. I wait for the sound to finish, then set my heel on the first plank. It rings, then holds.

A boot scuffs the rail above me, closer than the lane allowed. A man's weight shifts on the cap, and a single breath drops through the gap between the planks, short and sour with drink, crossing the skin of my neck like a draft under a door. I do not lift my hands. In one motion my heel slides a finger's width onto the plank's seam, where the wood is silent, and my fingertip presses the iron head beside the post, hard enough that the metal bites the pad. The boot scrapes once on wet wood and stops. The breath passes. Someone spits into the water, and the wake takes it.

The post's head is where I left it. The seam beside it is a hair wider on the left. The course trails into the seam and stops.

I lay the blade's flat into the seam and ease the plank a fraction. Beneath it the stringer is chilled, and the wood smells of tar and old rain. I feel for the folio's last leaf with two fingertips. The scrap is there, folded twice, the cord drawn through the stitch. I wait for the next groan before I touch it. One breath. Two. The grit of the wood sits under my nail.

I slide my fingertip under the scrap's crease. The edge is cool. I ease the cord back through the stitch a hair at a time, and it slips free without a snap. The scrap slides out flat beneath the blade. I close my hand around it and hold still.

On the folio's back leaf there is a second mark, a dent no wider than a thumbprint, pressed from behind. I trace it with my nail. The paper is warm there.

I unfold the scrap in my palm. My own figure, small and square, the corrected digit. Beside it, faint, Vesh's touch has left its shine. He has read it and accepted it.

I lay the rule down on the rail's cap. Its edge is cold against my wrist, and the chill climbs to my elbow and stops.

I take the coin from my coat and lay it beside the folio, nick turned up, its edge tucked flush under the corner. The nick warms under my thumb as I hold it there. Then I draw a fresh length of waxed cord through the seam and loop it once round the stitch.

Three actions, one breath, and I let the breath go slow as my nail sets the scrap's crease against the iron head, the paper's tooth catching the edge in a grit that holds, the fibres bending and not yet yielding, until the crease gives and lies flat under the leaf, while the rule's edge stays cold against my wrist, and the coin's nick warms beneath my other thumb, the metal holding the heat of my skin until the two temperatures are one, and the new loop draws through the seam with the waxed cord whispering over the stitch, the tar in the knot softening, then stiffening, as the tension takes it, and the loop gives its small tight yield the way a held rope gives before it bites, and the knot seats in the seam with a single soft click of wax against wood, the cord going still, while the lamp hisses through its crack, thin and steady, and the piles complain beneath the span, long and low, so the two sounds fall into the same breath, my thumbnail on the fold, the knot in its seat, the hiss and the complaint all closing on one count, and the planks give under my heel, then hold, and the bridge takes the sound into its timbers until the whole span is still.
